modules.title: Hyperkalaemia: don't miss the ECG, don't under-dose the calcium

bullets.text: Severe hyperkalaemia is usually defined as K+ 6.5 mmol/L or above
ECG progression: peaked T waves, then broad QRS, then sine wave, then arrest
A normal ECG does not exclude it — sensitivity is poor
Calcium gluconate 10% 30 mL IV to stabilise the myocardium. Repeat if no ECG change
Insulin 10 units with dextrose 25 g IV. Monitor glucose for at least 6 hours
Then treat the cause and consider potassium removal. Discuss with renal early

deep_dive.heading: Sequence at the bedside
steps: Attach continuous cardiac monitoring before anything else
12-lead ECG and repeat venous gas to confirm — rule out a haemolysed sample
Calcium first if there are ECG changes: it buys time but does not lower K+
Insulin-dextrose next: onset roughly 15 minutes, peak effect at about 1 hour
Salbutamol nebulisers are an adjunct only, never a substitute
Ask why: AKI, drugs (ACEi, ARB, spironolactone, trimethoprim), rhabdomyolysis, Addison's

quiz.question: A 72-year-old on ramipril and spironolactone is weak. K+ 7.1 mmol/L, ECG shows a broad QRS. Which drug goes in first?
quiz.explanation: Calcium stabilises the myocardium and is the first drug when there are ECG changes. It does not lower K+ — follow it immediately with insulin and dextrose.

source.title: Treatment of acute hyperkalaemia in adults

modules.title: Occlusion MI: the patterns that don't meet STEMI criteria

bullets.text: Millimetre STEMI criteria miss a substantial minority of acute occlusions
Posterior MI: horizontal ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves
Do posterior leads V7 to V9 — only 0.5 mm elevation is needed there
De Winter pattern: upsloping ST depression with tall symmetrical T waves
Modified Sgarbossa criteria apply when there is LBBB or a paced rhythm
Ongoing pain with a dynamic ECG warrants a cardiology conversation, not a wait

deep_dive.heading: What to do with the suspicion
points: Repeat the ECG every 10 to 15 minutes while pain continues
Compare with any previous ECG before calling a change new
Record posterior and right-sided leads and label them clearly on the trace
Escalate on the pattern and the story, not on whether the millimetres are met

quiz.question: Chest pain, ECG shows 2 mm horizontal ST depression in V1 to V3 with tall R waves and upright T waves. Next step?
options: Record posterior leads V7 to V9
Repeat troponin at 3 hours and reassess
quiz.explanation: This is the mirror image of posterior injury. Posterior leads confirm it, and only 0.5 mm of elevation in V7 to V9 is required.

modules.title: Anaphylaxis: IM adrenaline early, and what to do when it doesn't work

bullets.text: Adult dose: adrenaline 500 micrograms IM into the anterolateral thigh
Repeat every 5 minutes if there is no improvement
Refractory means no improvement after two appropriate IM doses
Refractory anaphylaxis needs an adrenaline infusion and expert help
Lay the patient flat — sitting or standing up has been linked to arrest
Steroids are no longer routinely recommended in the initial treatment

deep_dive.heading: If two IM doses have not worked
steps: Call for senior and critical care help now
Start an adrenaline infusion per your local protocol and stop repeat IM dosing
Give a rapid IV fluid bolus — distributive shock is often profound
Consider whether this is airway obstruction requiring immediate intervention
Observe after recovery: biphasic reactions occur, so follow local observation periods
Serial mast cell tryptase, adrenaline autoinjector, and an allergy referral before discharge

quiz.question: An adult with anaphylaxis has had two doses of IM adrenaline 5 minutes apart with no improvement. What is the next step?
options: Start an adrenaline infusion and call for critical care help
quiz.explanation: This is refractory anaphylaxis. Guidance moves to an adrenaline infusion with expert help rather than continued repeat IM dosing.

source.title: Emergency treatment of anaphylaxis: guidelines for healthcare providers

modules.title: Adult DKA: the four things that go wrong in the first two hours

bullets.text: Fixed rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour — weight-based, not a standard rate
Continue long-acting basal insulin. Stopping it causes rebound ketosis
Add glucose-containing fluid once blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L
Potassium falls fast — check it early and replace within the infusion
Resolution is ketone and pH based, not glucose based
Euglycaemic DKA happens on SGLT2 inhibitors — check ketones despite normal glucose

deep_dive.heading: Traps worth naming at handover
points: Do not withhold potassium replacement waiting for a formal lab result if the gas shows it
Bicarbonate is not routine and can worsen intracellular acidosis
A rising glucose on treatment usually means the infusion is not actually running
Look for the precipitant: infection, missed insulin, MI, pregnancy, drugs

quiz.question: A patient in DKA on an SGLT2 inhibitor has a blood glucose of 9 mmol/L. Which statement is correct?
options: DKA is excluded by the normal glucose
Euglycaemic DKA is recognised and ketones must be checked
Insulin should be withheld until glucose exceeds 14 mmol/L
Only sodium bicarbonate will correct the acidosis
quiz.explanation: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause DKA with near-normal glucose. Diagnosis rests on ketones and acidosis, and treatment runs with glucose-containing fluid alongside insulin.

source.title: The management of diabetic ketoacidosis in adults
source.publisher: Joint British Diabetes Societies for Inpatient Care

bullets.text: Bolus 10 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid, then reassess before the next one
Reassess after every bolus: heart rate, perfusion, conscious level, liver edge
Look for crackles, a new gallop or an enlarging liver — signs of fluid overload
In DKA and severe malnutrition the approach is different — follow those pathways
If shock persists after 40 to 60 mL/kg, think inotropes and critical care, not more fluid
Weight: use the child's actual weight if known, otherwise an age-based formula

deep_dive.heading: Why the volume changed
points: Practice moved away from routine 20 mL/kg boluses towards smaller volumes with reassessment
The concern is fluid overload and delayed recognition of the child who needs vasoactive support
The reassessment matters more than the number — a bolus given without review is the real error
Get the vasoactive drug conversation started early rather than after the fourth bolus

quiz.question: A 4-year-old with septic shock remains tachycardic and poorly perfused after 40 mL/kg of crystalloid. What is the priority?
options: Start vasoactive support and involve critical care
Wait for the lactate to return
quiz.explanation: Persisting shock after substantial fluid should prompt vasoactive support and critical care involvement rather than continued escalating boluses.

source.title: Sepsis: recognition, diagnosis and early management (NG51)

modules.title: Fever under 3 months: the ones you do not send home

bullets.text: Under 3 months with fever 38°C or above is a red flag in its own right
Serious bacterial infection can present with no localising signs at all
The traffic light system does not apply below 3 months in the usual way
Hypothermia in a neonate is as concerning as fever
A well-looking baby who fed poorly overnight still needs a senior review
Document the parental concern — it is a recognised risk marker

deep_dive.heading: At the whiteboard
points: Ask what has changed at home: feeding, wet nappies, tone, colour, cry
Check the observations against age-specific ranges, not adult intuition
Follow the local neonatal sepsis pathway for investigations and antibiotic timing
If you are discharging any infant under 3 months, that decision is a senior one

quiz.question: A 6-week-old has a temperature of 38.2°C, is feeding normally and looks well. What is the correct approach?
options: Follow the under-3-month febrile infant pathway with senior involvement
Reassure — the traffic light system says green
quiz.explanation: Age under 3 months with fever is a high-risk feature regardless of appearance. Local febrile infant pathways and senior review apply.

source.title: Fever in under 5s: assessment and initial management (NG143)

modules.title: Aortic dissection: the presentations that look like something else

bullets.text: Pain is often abrupt and maximal at onset rather than crescendo
Beware the stroke, limb ischaemia or syncope with chest or back pain
A normal chest X-ray and a normal D-dimer do not exclude it
Inferior ST elevation can be dissection involving the right coronary ostium
Ask about pulse and blood pressure differences, but their absence proves nothing
If you are seriously considering it, the test is a CT aortogram

deep_dive.heading: The trap worth naming
points: Anticoagulating a dissection as an ACS is the classic catastrophic error
Malperfusion syndromes explain the odd neurological or abdominal presentation
Control heart rate and blood pressure once suspected, and discuss with vascular or cardiothoracics early
Document explicitly why you did or did not image — it is a common complaint theme

quiz.question: A 58-year-old has sudden severe chest pain radiating to the back and a new right hemiparesis. BP differs by 30 mmHg between arms. What is the priority investigation?
quiz.explanation: Sudden chest and back pain with neurological deficit suggests dissection with carotid malperfusion. CT aortogram is the diagnostic test, and thrombolysis would be dangerous.

modules.title: Thunderclap headache: what the 6-hour CT does and does not do

bullets.text: Non-contrast CT within 6 hours of onset has very high sensitivity for SAH
That performance depends on a modern scanner and a competent reporter
Beyond 6 hours, sensitivity falls and further investigation is needed
LP is timed at 12 hours or more from onset to allow xanthochromia to form
Send CSF for spectrophotometry, and protect the sample from light
Onset time is the anchor for everything — pin it down precisely

deep_dive.heading: The conversation with the patient
points: Explain the residual risk if they decline the LP, and document that discussion
CT angiography is an alternative pathway in some units — know what yours does
A traumatic tap is not a reason to stop thinking; red cell counts alone are unreliable
Consider the alternatives: dissection, venous sinus thrombosis, reversible vasoconstriction

quiz.question: A patient presents 9 hours after a thunderclap headache. Non-contrast CT head is normal. What is appropriate?
options: Discharge — a normal CT excludes SAH
Plan LP at 12 hours or more from headache onset, or an agreed local alternative pathway
quiz.explanation: Beyond 6 hours a normal CT does not exclude SAH. LP is timed at 12 hours or more from onset so xanthochromia can be detected, unless your unit uses a CTA-based pathway.

modules.title: Paracetamol overdose: the questions that change management

bullets.text: Single time of ingestion, or staggered over more than an hour? It changes everything
The UK uses a single treatment line on the nomogram at 4 hours post-ingestion
Levels before 4 hours cannot be interpreted on the nomogram
Staggered and unknown-time overdoses are treated without waiting for a level
Check TOXBASE for the current regimen — it has changed more than once
Do not stop acetylcysteine for a rash alone; treat and continue

deep_dive.heading: Before the patient leaves
points: End-of-treatment bloods matter: ALT, INR, creatinine and a paracetamol level
Rising ALT or INR means continuing treatment and a liver unit conversation
Every overdose gets a mental health assessment and a capacity-aware risk discussion
Ask about co-ingestants, and about what the patient expected to happen

quiz.question: A patient took paracetamol in unknown amounts over about 8 hours. What is the correct approach?
options: Treat as a staggered overdose without waiting for a level, per TOXBASE
Plot the level on the nomogram from the first tablet
quiz.explanation: The nomogram only applies to a single ingestion at a known time. Staggered overdoses are managed on the TOXBASE pathway without relying on a plotted level.

modules.title: Head injury: the anticoagulated patient and the 'minor' bang

bullets.text: Anticoagulation changes the threshold for imaging even without other risk factors
Ask what they are on: DOAC, warfarin, antiplatelet — they are not equivalent
Falls in older people are frequently under-triaged as minor
Reduced GCS with no history is a head injury until proven otherwise
Know your reversal pathway and where the agents are kept before you need them
Discharge advice must be given to someone who will actually be with the patient

deep_dive.heading: Things that get missed
points: The mechanism was not trivial if the patient could not protect themselves on the way down
Consider why they fell — syncope, arrhythmia, sepsis, medication
Chronic subdural presents as confusion or unsteadiness weeks later, not as a headache
Check the C-spine properly in the older patient; injuries there are commonly missed

quiz.question: An 82-year-old on apixaban had an unwitnessed fall, hit her head, and is fully alert with no focal deficit. What is the appropriate action?
options: CT head in line with the anticoagulated head injury pathway
quiz.explanation: Anticoagulation lowers the imaging threshold in head injury. A normal GCS does not exclude significant intracranial bleeding in this group.

source.title: Head injury: assessment and early management (NG232)

modules.title: Testicular torsion: the clock started before they arrived

bullets.text: Acute scrotal pain in a young male is torsion until surgically excluded
Salvage rates fall steeply with time from onset of pain
Abdominal or groin pain with no scrotal complaint still needs the testes examined
Ultrasound must never delay a surgical opinion
Intermittent pain that has settled is still a torsion story
Document the examination, including that you examined at all

deep_dive.heading: Why this keeps appearing in claims
points: Pain referred to the abdomen leads to the genitalia never being examined
A normal-looking scrotum early on gives false reassurance
Waiting for a scan out of hours is a recurring cause of delay
Adolescents may not volunteer the symptom — ask directly and offer a chaperone

quiz.question: A 14-year-old has 3 hours of lower abdominal pain and vomiting. What must be part of the assessment?
options: Discharge with a surgical review in the morning
quiz.explanation: Torsion frequently presents as abdominal pain. Failure to examine the testes in a boy with abdominal pain is a well-documented cause of delayed diagnosis.

modules.title: Preoxygenation: the three minutes that decide how the RSI goes

bullets.text: Sit the patient up unless there is a specific reason not to
A well-sealed mask matters more than the flow rate on the flowmeter
Nasal cannulae left on during laryngoscopy extend safe apnoea time
The shocked and acidotic patient desaturates fast — plan for it, don't be surprised
Say the plan aloud: who does what, and what happens if the first look fails
Have push-dose vasopressor drawn up before induction, not after

deep_dive.heading: The 60 seconds before you push drugs
steps: Position: ear to sternal notch, head up
Preoxygenate with a tight seal and add nasal oxygen underneath
Optimise haemodynamics first — fluid or vasopressor before induction
State the plan A, B, C out loud and name who does each
Confirm suction is working and within reach of the intubator
Confirm the failed-airway equipment is open and the person who will use it knows

quiz.question: Which intervention most reliably prolongs safe apnoea time during laryngoscopy?
options: Increasing the tidal volume of bag-mask breaths
Leaving nasal cannula oxygen running through the apnoeic period
quiz.explanation: Apnoeic oxygenation via nasal cannulae maintained through laryngoscopy extends the time to desaturation, particularly in patients with limited reserve.
